3. Then AME Metro Editor Harry Rosenfeld offered me a lower salary than I was earning and told me, "I'm not saying to you, take it or leave it. I'm saying, please take it." The salary offered me was at the 3rd year experience level under the collective bargaining agreement. Because I had at least 3 years experience as a reporter and writer, I attempted to negotiate a higher salary, i.e., at the 4th year experience level. The Post would not agree. I began work in July 1972 at a weekly rate of $210 (or $10,920 per year)--$57 a week less than I was making previously.² I believe that men hired at about the same time were given increases to come to the Post and were not asked to take pay cuts.

4. My first job at the Post was as a city staff reporter, general assignments³ in the Metro Section. As a city reporter, I got off to a fast start and was assigned to Capital Hill to cover D.C. and metro area legislation. I covered the passage of home rule which came during a period when the newspaper was preoccupied with Watergate. Home rule passed Congress in 1973.

5. My next assignment was to cover Montgomery County, where I worked for Maryland editor Herbert Denton. Herb got along poorly with several reporters, myself included. Herb wanted me off his staff, as I learned in a meeting with Len Downie (then AME Metro) and Herb in which they tried to persuade me to quit.

6. Len Downie called me in and told me that they thought I wasn't right for the job and put me on night

14. Financial AME Pete Silberner hired me permanently for Financial (in April 1980). I covered beats including computers, the Securities and Exchange Commission and the tax-writing committees on Capitol Hill.

15. AME Frank Swoboda asked me to serve as editor of Washington Business, and I did beginning in January 1985. Prior to this, the Deputy AME Jerry Knight had been editing Washington Business. For that promotion, I received a $50 weekly pay increase (or approx. 5.75%) pursuant to the collective bargaining agreement. In this position, I served as editor of Washington Business (a Monday tabloid) and served as the assignment editor, directing local business coverage, including local financial coverage of the savings and local scandal.

16. During 1986, I was replaced as Washington Business Editor by Don Brazeal, who had recently come to the Post as a copy editor. Swoboda told me that he was not displacing me because of any issues with the job I was doing, but because Len Downie, then managing editor, wanted Brazeal in an assignment editor job. In 1995, Brazeal suddenly left Digital Ink, the Post's online operation, to "go on sabbatical" from which he never returned.

17. Subsequent to leaving the Washington Business and daily editing post at Swoboda's request, I served as editor of the Sunday Business Section. Swoboda described my new assignment in a personnel announcement as being "the nanny" for the section. After a short period, I asked to go back to reporting, because editing this section was less than a full-time job.

18. In 1986, I was a Washington Post reporter-in-residence fellow at Duke University for a month.

CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Explanation:
In 2000, Hilzenrath was given roughly a 10 percent salary increase and was put on the fast-track to prevent him from accepting a lucrative job offer. This salary increase is the reason for the salary disparity that begins in 2000.

Jerralld Knight

Jerralld Knight was paid more than Hamilton on the 1992 to 1999 salary snapshots and substantially more than Hamilton on the 2000 to 2002 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
Knight came to The Post in the late 1970s as a reporter in Financial News. He became the Deputy Editor in Financial News in 1982, returning to his reporter position in 1988. Prior to starting at The Post, Knight worked as a reporter for the Trenton Times for approximately two years. He also worked as a reporter for the Des Moines Register and the Ames Daily Tribune for a total of seven years. In addition, he was the Associate Editor for both the Discount Store News and the National Home Center News for approximately three years. Knight is a graduate of Iowa State University.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Knight received approximately a 30 percent increase over his prior salary at the Trenton Times. His starting salary was slightly less than the salary of Hamilton at that time.

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Knight had received 14 merit increases - nine of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these nine merit increases in the following years: 1978, 1980, 1981, 1997, 1998, 2000, 2001 and 2002. Knight also received a promotional increase when he became the Deputy Editor in Financial in 1982.

Explanation:
Knight was a Deputy Editor in Financial News from 1982 to 1988 - a position of great responsibility. He retained his editor's salary when he returned to Financial News as a reporter.

Knight writes an important investigative column on local businesses for the Monday Business Section - a column The Post values greatly. He also writes a daily column that appears on washpost.com and he appears daily on a local television network affiliate to discuss the stock market as a representative of The Post.

The Post could not locate information about Munson's prior salary at The Wall Street Journal. His starting salary was less than the salary of Skrzycki at that time.

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Munson had received 13 merit increases - seven of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these seven merit increases in the following years: 1991, 1992, 1993, 1998 and 1999. Munson also received substantial salary increases when he became the Assistant Editor and Deputy Editor in Outlook in 2002.

Explanation:
Munson's salary increased during the time he was the Bureau Chief in China - a position of great responsibility. He retained this salary when he returned to Financial News as a Wall Street/SEC Investigative reporter.

Munson later moved to National as a State Department reporter and is now the Deputy Editor of Outlook.

Robert O'Harrow

Robert O'Harrow, in his first stint in Financial News, was paid substantially less than Hamilton and Mayer as noted on the 1998 salary snapshot. When he returned to Financial News after a stint with the Investigative Staff, O'Harrow was paid substantially more than Hamilton and more than Mayer on the 2000 to 2002 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
O'Harrow came to The Post on in the early 1980s as a copy aide. He resigned from that position in 1985. O'Harrow returned to The Post in the early 1990s as a reporter in the Loudon Bureau later transferring to the Fairfax Bureau. He became a reporter in Financial News in 1997. He began a roughly year-and-a-half stint in 1998 with the Investigative Staff, returning to Financial News as a reporter in 2000. Prior to starting at The Post as a reporter, O'Harrow worked as a reporter for The Record for 16 months. He also worked as a reporter for The Times-Herald Record for approximately three-and-a-half years. O'Harrow is a graduate of Virginia Tech University.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, O'Harrow received approximately a 29 percent increase over his prior salary. His starting salary was substantially less than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at that time.
